name: Noni
confidence_why: Hyman's 1981 grammar describes Noni as a three-level tone language with contrastive tone on every syllable and says nothing about stress, and the only other first-hand description, Richards's 1991 Paris thesis, agrees that Noone is tonal but its abstract (the only part of it available) adds that stress is phonologically distinctive and confines contour tones and complex segments to stressed sylla…
catalog_citation: Hyman, Larry M. 1981. Noni Grammatical Structure, with Special Reference to Verb Morphology. Southern California Occasional Papers in Linguistics (SCOPIL) 9. Los Angeles: Department of Linguistics, University of Southern California. vi+121 pp.
catalog_locator: Part I: Phonology, Chapter 2 'The Tone System', section 1, printed p. 5 = pdf page 11 of the scan (saved render; scanned). Chapter 1 'The Sound System', printed pp. 1-4 (pdf pp. 7-10), has no stress statement either.
catalog_quote: 1. Each syllable carries contrastive tone in Noni. Three level (register) tones characterize the language: H (high), M (mid) and L (low). These three levels are represented by means of the three accent marks á, ā and à, as seen in the following examples: ... The language also makes use of a number of contour tones involving a change from one of the three tone levels to another within the same syllable. Of the six logical possibilities (LH, LM, MH, HL, MH, ML), only MH does not exist in the language. The remaining five contour tones are all found on monosyllables, as in the following noun examples: ... Except in certain class 5 nouns, the HM contour tone is rare in Noni, as is the HL tone. LH, LM and ML all frequently occur on both nouns and verbs. Finally, two nouns have been found with a complex rising-falling (LHL) tone ... In all cases the domain of tone is the syllable. Thus, in syllables beginning with a NC sequence, the nasal always carries the phonetic pitch of the beginning point of the tone of its syllable
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule for word stress is given. The only accessible primary description (Hyman 1981) treats Noni as a three-level register tone language (H, M, L plus LH, LM, HL, HM, ML contours, and a rare LHL) with the syllable as the tone-bearing unit; a full-text search for stress/accent the scanned of all 127 scanned pages for stress/accent/prominence/intensity finds no phonological statement about stress (the word 'accent' occurs only as 'accent marks' for tone; 'prominence' on printed pp. 105-106 is syntactic focus). Hyman also notes there is no downdrift (Ch. 2 section 2, p. 6).
new_statements.exceptions: None relevant; tonal notes only (LH realized LM before H/L/pause; M optionally lowered between L_H and H_L; nouns keep isolation tones in context, verbs alternate tonally by tense/aspect).
new_statements.domain_note: This is a tone statement, not a stress statement: the source is silent on stress. Domain of tone = the syllable; nouns cited in isolation (citation forms) and in phrase context.
new_statements.identity_note: Hyman 1981 describes 'Noni' as spoken at Nkor (consultant Mark Bintum of Nkor); this is the language-level noon1243 (Glottolog alternate names Noni, Nooni, Kumaju), no dialect issue. The only other open Beboid description downloaded, Boutwell 2020, is a grammar of Nchane (ncha1245), a different Beboid language, and was used only for context and bibliography.

new_statements.quote: Une attention toute particuliere est portee au role joue par l'accent, en rapport avec la fonction du ton et la distribution des differents types d'unites consonantiques et vocaliques constituant les schemes syllabiques. [...] ces schemes sont alors classes selon la place de l'accent. [...] Elle permet aussi de rendre compte des restrictions distributionnelles et combinatoires observees au niveau des tons modules et des unites complexes (consonnes prenasalisees, labialisees ou palatalisees ; voyelles longues ou nasales), qui n'apparaissent generalement qu'en syllabe accentuee. Ces restrictions ne pourraient pas s'expliquer de maniere non-arbitraire et satisfaisante si l'accent etait considere comme un trait non-pertinent au niveau de la phonologie.
new_statements.translation: Special attention is given to the role played by stress, in relation to the function of tone and to the distribution of the different types of consonant and vowel units making up the syllable patterns. [...] these patterns are then classified according to the place of stress. [...] It also accounts for the distributional and combinatory restrictions observed on contour tones and on complex units (prenasalized, labialized or palatalized consonants; long or nasal vowels), which generally appear only in a stressed syllable. These restrictions could not be explained in a non-arbitrary and satisfactory way if stress were regarded as a non-relevant feature at the phonological level.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's Hyman 1981 statement (three-level tone language, no stress statement) but adds a claim Hyman does not make: that Noone has phonologically distinctive stress interacting with tone, with contour tones and complex segments limited to stressed syllables. Placement is not recoverable from the abstract; the 605-page thesis itself is not online (theses.fr: accessible = non). Covers three languages: Noone (noon1243), Ncanti (= Nchane/Ncane, ncha1245) and Sali (Nsari, sari1244).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Abstract only: Noone (with Ncanti and Sali) is described as a tone language in which stress ('accent') is nevertheless a phonologically relevant, distinctive feature; syllable patterns are classified by the position of the stressed syllable, and contour tones and complex segments (prenasalized/labialized/palatalized consonants, long or nasal vowels) are generally confined to the stressed syllable. The abstract does not say where in the word stress falls.
new_statements.exceptions: none stated; 'generalement' (generally) hedges the stressed-syllable restriction
new_statements.identity_note: Hyman 1981 = Noni of Nkor (consultant Mark Bintum). Richards 1991 covers Noone (noon1243) together with Ncanti (= Nchane, ncha1245) and Sali (= Nsari, sari1244); the abstract makes one claim for all three, not a Noone-specific one. Lux 2016 is the SIL Nooni dictionary (ISO nhu), same language.

new_statements.translation: Special attention is paid to the role played by stress, in relation to the function of tone and to the distribution of the different types of consonant and vowel units making up the syllable patterns. The descriptions start from canonical syllable types, which combine into patterns of different lengths; these patterns are then classified according to the place of the stress. [...] contour tones and complex units (prenasalized, labialized or palatalized consonants; long or nasal vowels), which generally appear only in a stressed syllable. These restrictions could not be explained in a non-arbitrary and satisfactory way if stress were treated as a non-distinctive feature at the phonological level.

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog codes Noni 'tonal' from Hyman 1981 (three level tones, every syllable tone-bearing, no stress statement). Richards' abstract keeps the tonal analysis and adds distinctive stress interacting with tone (stressed syllable = licensing position for contour tones and complex segments). Same content as existing statement no. 2 held by the project (verified, from this same abstract) - agrees with it; placement still unknown, so no fixed-position reading can be assigned.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Noone (with Ncanti and Sali) is analysed as a tone language in which stress ('accent') is ALSO phonologically distinctive: syllable patterns of words are classified by where the stress falls, and contour tones, complex consonants and long/nasal vowels are generally licensed only in the stressed syllable. The abstract does not say which syllable is stressed (placement not recoverable without the thesis).
new_statements.exceptions: 'generalement' (generally) - the restriction of contour tones/complex units to stressed syllables has exceptions, unspecified in the abstract
new_statements.identity_note: Hyman 1981 describes Noni of Nkor village (consultant Mark Bintum); Richards 1991 treats Noone together with Ncanti (= Nchane, ncha1245) and Sali (= Nsari/Saari) as Eastern Beboid languages of the North-West Province; the Webonary dictionary is SIL's Nooni (ISO nhu) community orthography dictionary (Lux, with Elijah Ntani Fale). All are the same language, Noone [noon1243].

readall_conflicts: No direct contradiction. Hyman 1981 (catalog source, read earlier from the full scan) describes Noni as a three-level tone language and says nothing about stress. The Richards 1991 abstract (the only part of that work obtainable) asserts that stress is a phonologically distinctive feature in Noone, Ncanti and Sali, classifies syllable patterns by stress placement, and restricts contour tones and complex segments to stressed syllables — a functionalist (Martinet-school) analysis that Hyman's autosegmental description does not engage with. Whether Richards' 'accent' corresponds to word-level stress in the catalog's sense, and where it falls, cannot be settled without the thesis text. The Lux 2016 Webonary dictionary could not be opened (not reachable by automated download), so its front matter (which may include an orthography/tone note) remains unchecked.
